headings.title: Introduction and Definition of Insomnia
headings.content: Insomnia is one of the most common sleep disorders encountered in clinical practice, characterized by difficulty initiating sleep, difficulty maintaining sleep, or waking up too early with an inability to return to sleep. For nursing students in Nigeria, understanding insomnia requires recognizing that it is not merely a symptom, but a complex condition that significantly impairs daytime functioning, mood, and overall quality of life. Patients suffering from insomnia often report feeling unrefreshed despite an adequate opportunity to sleep. It is vital to differentiate between transient insomnia, which may last a few days due to acute stress or environmental changes, and chronic insomnia, which persists for at least three nights per week for over three months. As future nurses, you will care for patients whose insomnia is exacerbated by hospital environments, physiological pain, psychological distress, or socioeconomic factors prevalent in our setting. Proper assessment and management of sleep disturbances promote faster physical recovery, reduce hospital length of stay, and prevent long-term health complications such as hypertension, diabetes, and mood disorders.

headings.title: Normal Sleep Physiology and Circadian Rhythms
headings.content: Normal human sleep architecture alternates cyclically between Non-Rapid Eye Movement (NREM) sleep and Rapid Eye Movement (NREM) sleep. NREM sleep is further divided into three stages (N1, N2, and N3), transitioning from light sleep to deep, restorative slow-wave sleep (N3), which is crucial for physical tissue repair and immune function. REM sleep is characterized by vivid dreaming, high brain activity, and muscle atonia, playing a critical role in memory consolidation and cognitive processing. A typical adult sleep cycle lasts approximately 90 to 110 minutes, repeating 4 to 6 times per night. Circadian rhythms, regulated by the suprachiasmatic nucleus of the hypothalamus, act as the body's internal biological clock. This master pacemaker synchronizes physiological processes with the 24-hour light-dark cycle primarily through the secretion of melatonin from the pineal gland in response to darkness. Disruptions to this delicate hormonal and neurological balance—such as night shift work common among healthcare professionals, jet lag, or exposure to blue light from screens before bed—can desynchronize the circadian rhythm, leading to severe difficulty falling or staying asleep.

headings.title: Classification and Types of Insomnia
headings.content: Insomnia is broadly classified into two major categories: primary (or idiopathic) insomnia and secondary (or comorbid) insomnia. Primary insomnia occurs independently without any direct association with a coexisting medical, psychiatric, or substance use disorder. Conversely, secondary insomnia is much more prevalent in clinical settings and is directly linked to underlying conditions. These can include psychiatric disorders like major depressive disorder and generalized anxiety disorders, medical illnesses causing chronic pain, cardiovascular disease, respiratory distress, or neurologic conditions. Additionally, substance-induced insomnia can result from the use, abuse, or withdrawal of prescription medications, alcohol, caffeine, or illicit substances. Nurses must thoroughly evaluate patients to determine whether sleep disruption is an isolated problem or a secondary manifestation of another underlying pathological or environmental issue, as treatment approaches differ significantly between the two classifications.

headings.title: Pathophysiology and Etiology of Insomnia
headings.content: The pathophysiology of insomnia is largely understood through the lens of hyperarousal—a state of persistent physiological, cognitive, and cortical activation that prevents normal sleep initiation and maintenance. Patients with chronic insomnia exhibit elevated metabolic rates, increased heart rates, elevated core body temperatures, and heightened levels of stress hormones such as cortisol and adrenocorticotropic hormone throughout both day and night. Spielman’s 3P Model is the classic framework used to explain insomnia etiology, consisting of Predisposing factors (such as biological traits or genetic vulnerability), Precipitating factors (such as acute life stressors, illness, or hospitalization), and Perpetuating factors (such as maladaptive behavioral changes like staying in bed while awake, napping during the day, or excessive worry about sleep). While predisposing and precipitating factors set the stage, nursing interventions primarily target perpetuating factors to break the cycle of chronic insomnia.

headings.title: Clinical Manifestations and Patient Assessment
headings.content: Clinical assessment of a patient presenting with insomnia requires a comprehensive nursing history, physical examination, and psychological evaluation. Nurses should utilize validated tools such as the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) or the Insomnia Severity Index (ISI) to quantify the severity of the sleep disturbance and its impact on daytime functioning. A detailed sleep diary maintained by the patient for one to two weeks provides invaluable objective data regarding sleep-onset latency, nighttime awakenings, total sleep time, daytime fatigue, and the use of substances like caffeine or alcohol. Nurses must also assess for contributing physical symptoms such as pain, nocturia, or dyspnea, as well as signs of underlying depression or anxiety. Evaluating the patient's medication list is crucial, as many prescription and over-the-counter drugs can disrupt sleep architecture. Through active listening and careful observation, the nurse can identify specific triggers and tailor individualized care plans.

headings.title: Diagnostic Evaluation and Sleep Studies
headings.content: While routine diagnostic testing is not always necessary for uncomplicated insomnia, diagnostic evaluations become essential when secondary sleep disorders are suspected. Polysomnography (PSG) is the gold standard overnight sleep study conducted in a specialized sleep laboratory, recording electroencephalography (EEG), electrooculography (EOG), electromyography (EMG), electrocardiography (ECG), and respiratory airflow. PSG is particularly indicated if clinicians suspect obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), periodic limb movement disorder (PLMD), or narcolepsy, rather than primary insomnia. Another diagnostic tool is wrist actigraphy, a non-invasive watch-like device worn by the patient for several weeks to estimate rest-activity cycles in a natural home environment. Blood tests may also be ordered to rule out metabolic or endocrine abnormalities such as hyperthyroidism or anemia that can impair normal sleep. As nurses, explaining these procedures to patients helps reduce anxiety and ensures accurate data collection.

headings.title: Pharmacological Management and Nursing Considerations
headings.content: Pharmacological management of insomnia is typically recommended for short-term use due to risks of tolerance, dependence, abuse, and adverse side effects. Commonly prescribed medications include Benzodiazepine Receptor Agonists (BZRAs) such as diazepam or temazepam, and Non-benzodiazepine receptor agonists (often called Z-drugs like zolpidem), which help reduce sleep-onset latency. Melatonin receptor agonists, such as ramelteon, and certain sedating antidepressant medications (e.g., trazodone or low-dose doxepin) are also utilized, especially when insomnia is comorbid with depression or anxiety. Over-the-counter options, including antihistamines like diphenhydramine, are widely available but generally discouraged for chronic use due to anticholinergic side effects, daytime grogginess, and tolerance build-up, particularly in elderly patients where they increase fall risks. Nursing responsibilities include monitoring for side effects such as morning sedation, respiratory depression, complex sleep behaviors (e.g., sleepwalking or driving while asleep), educating patients on safe usage, and advising against abrupt cessation or mixing sedatives with alcohol.

headings.title: Non-Pharmacological Interventions and Sleep Hygiene
headings.content: Non-pharmacological interventions are the first-line treatment recommended by clinical guidelines for chronic insomnia because they target underlying behavioral and cognitive perpetuating factors with lasting results. Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia (CBT-I) is the gold standard psychological treatment, incorporating cognitive restructuring, stimulus control therapy, and sleep restriction therapy. Stimulus control trains the brain to associate the bed and bedroom exclusively with sleep and sexual activity—instructing patients to get out of bed if they cannot sleep for more than 20 minutes. Sleep restriction therapy temporarily limits time spent in bed to match actual sleep duration, thereby increasing sleep efficiency. In addition to CBT-I, rigorous sleep hygiene education is essential. Nurses must teach patients to maintain a consistent wake-up time daily, avoid caffeine, nicotine, and heavy meals close to bedtime, engage in regular daytime exercise, and create a cool, dark, and quiet sleeping environment free from electronic devices.

headings.title: Complications of Chronic Insomnia
headings.content: When left untreated or unmanaged, chronic insomnia has profound physical, psychological, and social consequences. Prolonged sleep deprivation impairs cognitive function, reducing concentration, memory retention, decision-making abilities, and reaction times, which increases the risk of accidents and occupational errors. Emotionally, chronic insomnia significantly elevates the risk of developing or worsening mood disorders, particularly major depression, anxiety, and irritability. Physiologically, persistent sleep disturbances are linked to chronic systemic inflammation, weakened immune response, and endocrine dysregulation. Over time, chronic insomnia contributes to major health complications including hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, obesity, and cardiovascular events such as myocardial infarction and stroke. Recognizing these severe systemic outcomes emphasizes the critical role of nurses in advocating for early detection, comprehensive sleep assessments, and holistic management strategies for all patients.
